entries.snippet:
Anthropic has introduced a new 'auto mode' for Claude Code, designed to enhance workflow efficiency by allowing the AI tool to make certain permission decisions autonomously. Traditionally, Claude Code required user approval for many actions, potentially causing interruptions in longer coding tasks. With auto mode, permission requests are processed through a classifier that automatically allows safe actions and flags risky ones, such as file deletions, for user confirmation. This update aims to strike a balance between security and productivity, especially since some developers have been bypassing permissions altogether, creating security risks.

Currently available as a research preview, the feature may still misclassify actions due to contextual limitations—potentially allowing risky actions or blocking safe ones. The initial rollout is limited to Teams users, with future expansions expected for Enterprise and API users. Auto mode supports only the Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 models for now and is unlikely to work with earlier versions, though support for future versions is anticipated.
entries.title: Anthropic gives Claude Code new 'auto mode' which lets it choose its own permissions

entries.snippet: Anthropic, the company behind AI assistant Claude, has announced changes to its usage policy to better manage increasing demand, particularly during peak hours. Moving forward, users—including those on paid Pro and Max plans—will hit their five-hour session message limits more quickly during peak periods (5am–11am PT / 1pm–7pm GMT on weekdays), although overall weekly limits remain unchanged. This update affects approximately 7% of users, who are now advised to shift heavy usage to off-peak hours to optimize their allowance. The announcement came informally through an engineer on social media rather than an official company channel, raising concerns about transparency. This adjustment follows a recent, publicly announced increase in off-peak usage rates, highlighting how Claude’s pay-as-you-go model now requires more strategic planning. Users are encouraged to stay alert, as usage restrictions are becoming more dynamic and less predictable.
entries.title: Claude is limiting usage more aggressively during peak hours - here's what changed

entries.snippet:
Anthropic has introduced a new capability for its AI assistant Claude, allowing it to autonomously control a user's computer by simulating mouse and keyboard inputs. This feature integrates with third-party apps like Slack and Google Calendar via Claude Cowork and Claude Code, and it activates direct computer control only when those integrations are insufficient. Users initiate commands through the Dispatch app on their smartphones, enabling remote desktop interaction from their pockets.

To mitigate risks, Anthropic has embedded safeguards, including requiring user permissions and allowing manual override at any time. While this tool offers automation for tasks like checking email or generating reports, it remains in early stages and may be error-prone or slow compared to native integrations. The feature is currently restricted to macOS for users of the Claude Pro and Max tiers, and sensitive applications are limited from use due to privacy concerns. A wider rollout is possible after the testing phase.
entries.title: 'Put Claude to work': Claude can now use your computer autonomously, you just have to tell it what to do

entries.snippet: Anthropic has introduced an experimental "auto mode" for Claude Code, its AI-powered programming assistant. This new feature allows the AI to act autonomously in certain situations while implementing safeguards to reduce risk. Unlike earlier versions that either required constant human oversight or gave the AI too much unchecked control, auto mode offers a middle ground. It flags potentially harmful actions—such as deleting files, exposing sensitive data, or executing malicious code—and either stops them or prompts user intervention. Currently, auto mode is available as a research preview to users on the Team plan, with plans to expand access to Enterprise and API customers soon. Anthropic emphasizes that the feature is still experimental and advises developers to use it in secure, isolated environments, as it does not completely eliminate risk.
entries.title: Anthropic's Claude Code gets 'safer' auto mode

entries.snippet:
Anthropic has introduced a new feature in its Claude AI platform, allowing its Code and Cowork tools to autonomously control a user's computer. This includes performing actions such as opening files, navigating web browsers and apps, and running development tools on macOS systems. Announced as a research preview for Claude Pro and Max subscribers, the feature builds on autonomous capabilities initially introduced with Claude's 3.5 Sonnet AI model in 2024. It requires the Claude desktop app on macOS and pairing with the mobile app to function.

The system prioritizes using connectors with services like Slack and Google Workspace, but when unavailable, it can directly operate the user's computer interface—controlling the mouse, keyboard, and screen. Anthropic emphasizes that Claude will always seek explicit user permission before interacting with the computer. The tool works particularly well with a feature called Dispatch, which enables mobile-to-desktop task assignment. However, Anthropic notes that the AI may struggle with complex tasks and is sharing the functionality in an early stage to gather user feedback and understand its limitations.
entries.title: Anthropic's Claude Code and Cowork can control your computer

entries.snippet:
On March 25, 2026, the AI service Claude experienced a major partial outage, prompting a surge of reports on Downdetector, peaking at around 5,000. Users across the platform reported failed interactions with the chatbot, and screenshots showed error messages when trying to access the service. The issue didn’t appear to stem simply from user overload, indicating deeper technical problems.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, responded promptly by updating its status page. They acknowledged the outage and continued investigating the issue, although communication temporarily paused, leading to user frustration. Despite being labeled a “partial outage,” many users were unable to access the service at all.

Eventually, Anthropic issued a fix which began gradually restoring operations. Downdetector reports began to subside, signaling progress toward resolution, although additional issues such as elevated errors in the Claude Opus 4.6 model and Cowork tool were noted. By the end of the day, most services were recovering, with report numbers returning to near-normal levels. Users were encouraged to report whether Claude was functioning again, and Anthropic promised to closely monitor for further errors.
entries.title: Claude was down - Here's what happened why the AI service as out of order

entries.snippet:
Due to a significant surge in popularity, Anthropic has adjusted usage limits for its AI assistant Claude across free, Pro, and Max subscriptions. Although overall weekly limits remain unchanged, users will now hit their session caps faster during peak hours (5 am to 11 am PT), affecting about 7% of users—especially those with Pro subscriptions. Shifting heavy usage to off-peak times is advised to mitigate the effect.

This move comes as Anthropic grapples with the strain of increased demand and limited computational resources. Interest in Claude has spiked since CEO Dario Amodei’s decision not to grant the Pentagon unrestricted access to the company's AI models. The company continues to prioritize enterprise services while addressing infrastructure challenges amid the competitive AI landscape.

Other companies, including OpenAI, are similarly facing compute strains. OpenAI recently shut down its AI video app Sora to focus resources on core services. Amodei has criticized the high-risk strategies of rival firms investing heavily in mega data centers, underscoring Anthropic’s more cautious approach to scaling AI responsibly.

Yes — **that kind of workflow is possible**, but there is an important difference:

## What Claude is likely doing

It is **not** that Claude has a built-in magic “post everywhere” button by itself.

What is happening is usually this stack:

1. **Claude Code** writes/adapts the content.

items.snippet:
Anthropic has introduced a new 'auto mode' for Claude Code, designed to enhance workflow efficiency by allowing the AI tool to make certain permission decisions autonomously. Traditionally, Claude Code required user approval for many actions, potentially causing interruptions in longer coding tasks. With auto mode, permission requests are processed through a classifier that automatically allows safe actions and flags risky ones, such as file deletions, for user confirmation. This update aims to strike a balance between security and productivity, especially since some developers have been bypassing permissions altogether, creating security risks.

Currently available as a research preview, the feature may still misclassify actions due to contextual limitations—potentially allowing risky actions or blocking safe ones. The initial rollout is limited to Teams users, with future expansions expected for Enterprise and API users. Auto mode supports only the Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 models for now and is unlikely to work with earlier versions, though support for future versions is anticipated.

supporting_websites.snippet: Anthropic has introduced an experimental "auto mode" for Claude Code, its AI-powered programming assistant. This new feature allows the AI to act autonomously in certain situations while implementing safeguards to reduce risk. Unlike earlier versions that either required constant human oversight or gave the AI too much unchecked control, auto mode offers a middle ground. It flags potentially harmful actions—such as deleting files, exposing sensitive data, or executing malicious code—and either stops them or prompts user intervention. Currently, auto mode is available as a research preview to users on the Team plan, with plans to expand access to Enterprise and API customers soon. Anthropic emphasizes that the feature is still experimental and advises developers to use it in secure, isolated environments, as it does not completely eliminate risk.
supporting_websites.title: Anthropic's Claude Code gets 'safer' auto mode

supporting_websites.snippet:
Anthropic has introduced a new capability for its AI assistant Claude, allowing it to autonomously control a user's computer by simulating mouse and keyboard inputs. This feature integrates with third-party apps like Slack and Google Calendar via Claude Cowork and Claude Code, and it activates direct computer control only when those integrations are insufficient. Users initiate commands through the Dispatch app on their smartphones, enabling remote desktop interaction from their pockets.

To mitigate risks, Anthropic has embedded safeguards, including requiring user permissions and allowing manual override at any time. While this tool offers automation for tasks like checking email or generating reports, it remains in early stages and may be error-prone or slow compared to native integrations. The feature is currently restricted to macOS for users of the Claude Pro and Max tiers, and sensitive applications are limited from use due to privacy concerns. A wider rollout is possible after the testing phase.
supporting_websites.title: 'Put Claude to work': Claude can now use your computer autonomously, you just have to tell it what to do

supporting_websites.snippet:
Anthropic has introduced a new feature in its Claude AI platform, allowing its Code and Cowork tools to autonomously control a user's computer. This includes performing actions such as opening files, navigating web browsers and apps, and running development tools on macOS systems. Announced as a research preview for Claude Pro and Max subscribers, the feature builds on autonomous capabilities initially introduced with Claude's 3.5 Sonnet AI model in 2024. It requires the Claude desktop app on macOS and pairing with the mobile app to function.

The system prioritizes using connectors with services like Slack and Google Workspace, but when unavailable, it can directly operate the user's computer interface—controlling the mouse, keyboard, and screen. Anthropic emphasizes that Claude will always seek explicit user permission before interacting with the computer. The tool works particularly well with a feature called Dispatch, which enables mobile-to-desktop task assignment. However, Anthropic notes that the AI may struggle with complex tasks and is sharing the functionality in an early stage to gather user feedback and understand its limitations.
